subject: Sensitive header suppression & request/response pseudonymization - next steps
messages:

Subject: Sensitive header suppression & request/response pseudonymization - recap

Hi Sam — thanks again for taking time this morning. Quick recap from our discovery call and a set of concrete asks so we can put together a tailored proposal.

Call summary (brief):
- HealthTech is evaluating Redwood for user-facing document summarization and anonymized analytics pipelines.
- Primary concerns: PII leakage in request/response logs, trace IDs correlating to user identifiers, and retention policies for debug data.
- Compliance drivers: SOC2 + regional audit requirements for a US-hosted production deployment.

Open questions / asks (what we need from you):
1) Can you confirm the classes of PII you consider sensitive in logs beyond names/emails (e.g., patient IDs, device identifiers, internal account numbers)?
2) Which headers in your traffic are definitive identifiers we must suppress (Authorization, x-user-id, x-session-id, x-correlation-id)? Any custom headers?
3) Desired maximum retention for request/response payloads and for structured telemetry (30d/90d/custom)?
4) Do you require irreversible redaction (remove/replace with token) vs. reversible pseudonymization keyed to your HSM?

Next steps (our plan):
- Aditya will sketch two engineering approaches: header suppression + prefix-based KV cache scrubbing, and streaming pseudonymization for request/response bodies.
- We will attach a short sample log snippet showing recommended suppression and a draft redaction proposal for your security team.
- Schedule a follow-up to review the proposal and finalize retention SLAs.

Attachments: redaction-proposal-v1.pdf (draft), sample-logs-snippet.txt

Thanks — I’ll loop in Dev for technical clarifications.

—
Sofia Ivanova
Senior Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
sofia_ivanova@redwood.com

Sofia —

Following up with a couple more specifics from our security reviewers:
- Trace correlation: we cannot expose any header that can be used to link logs back to a patient or internal account. That includes x-correlation-id when correlated to user ref.
- Audit requirement: any reversible pseudonymization must be logged in an access-controlled audit trail (who requested de-pseudonymize + reason).

If you can provide two short examples:
A) Header-only suppression example (raw header -> sanitized header)
B) Body-level pseudonymization example (JSON payload with patient_id replaced by stable pseudonym)

We can share a sanitized sample production log if helpful.

Thanks — Sam
From: Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.com>
To: Sofia Ivanova <sofia_ivanova@redwood.com>, Sam Carroll <sam.carroll@healthtech.io>
Cc: Dev Patel <dev_patel@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
Date: Wed, 14 Apr 2027 14:30:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Sensitive header suppression & request/response pseudonymization - recap

Sam / Sofia — thanks for the clarity. Attaching a small sample (sample-logs-snippet.txt) and drafting two options we recommend:

Option A — Header suppression (low-effort, fast)
- Drop or mask problematic headers at the ingress edge: replace values with fixed token e.g. X-HT-User-Ref: [REDACTED-USER] and remove x-correlation-id from persisted logs when it maps to user refs.
- Pros: immediate, minimal latency, no key management.
- Cons: loses linkability for multi-request debugging.

Option B — Short-term reversible pseudonymization (for debug window <=72h) + irreversible redaction after TTL
- At ingestion, replace PII with HMAC-based pseudonym (HMAC(key, value)) where key is customer-specific and stored in their KMS/HSM.
- Keep a small encrypted mapping for TTL period (72h) only; after TTL, purge mappings and replace entries in persisted logs with irreversible redaction marker.
- Maintain audit trail for any re-identification requests (who/when/why).
- Pros: preserves short-term debugging without long-term risk.
- Cons: requires KMS integration and audit hooks.

Implementation notes / timeline:
- We can deliver Option A configuration in a PoC within 1 week (config + docs).
- Option B requires KMS work and an access-audit pipeline; estimate 3-4 weeks for a PoC depending on KMS integration complexity.

Sofia — I attached the two small artifacts and a short Jira ticket link for the engineering tasks: https://redwood-internal.atlassian.net/browse/INF-789
